Abstract Recent advances in the characterization of carbon-based materials for cutting-edge applications have highlighted the importance of understanding their physical, chemical, and electrochemical properties. These insights have led to the development of specific interrelations key surface-related parameters. Of particular interest is the relation between porous and non-porous carbon materials and their interfacial interactions with surrounding environments. For over two decades, the difference between the point of zero charge (pHPZC) and the isoelectric point (pH(I)) has been considered indicative of the surface charge distribution in porous carbons. Simultaneously, the increasing relevance of carbon materials in electrochemical systems has driven interest in the potential of zero charge (EPZC), which provides information on how the surface charge of an electrode responds to an applied electric potential, and how the surface potential responds to changes in the surface chemistry of the electrode. Considering the substantial influence of the surface chemistry on these three parameters, they are certainly correlated, which can be established based on theoretical and experimental fundamentals of pH(I), pHPZC, and EPZC. Unfortunately, to date, no single study has addressed all three parameters simultaneously; only partial correlations have been reported. This review aims to provide a comprehensive interpretation of these three physical properties using activated carbon (AC) as a reference material, given its extensive use in technological applications. Insights derived from AC provide a robust conceptual framework that can be extended to other carbonaceous systems, particularly in adsorption and electrochemical applications. Notably, the review contends that, although the parameters may not correlate directly, they can still be used together to more effectively explain interfacial phenomena in various carbon-based materials. * Previous * Next Keywords Point of zero charge Zeta-potential Isoelectric point Titration curves Activated carbon 1. Introduction Activated carbons (ACs) have been extensively developed and applied across diverse fields, including adsorption, catalysis, electrochemical processes, water treatment, gas purification, energy storage, and a variety of industrial applications [1,2]. Current research mainly attributes the performance of ACs to their textural properties, such as specific surface area, pore size distribution, and pore volume, as well as their chemical and electrical characteristics [3]. Consequently, considerable efforts and resources have been dedicated to characterizing and understanding the physical and chemical properties of these materials [4]. The surface chemistry of ACs is significantly influenced by the presence of heteroatoms within the graphitic layers [5]. Furthermore, the protonation and deprotonation of certain oxygenated surface groups can provide an electrostatic charge to the carbon surface [6]. The magnitude of this surface charge depends on the pH of the solution, and the pH at which the net surface charge of a solid is zero is referred as the point of zero charge (pHPZC) [7]. In addition, solids can be characterized by another parameter, the isoelectric point (pH(I)) [8], which corresponds to the pH at which the zeta potential (ζ) is zero. For non-porous solids, the pH(I) is widely used and typically close to the pHPZC. However, in porous solids, the pH(I) is usually lower than the pHPZC [9]. A complementary concept for understanding the charge distribution at the interface of an electrically polarized surface is the potential of zero charge (EPZC). While the pH(I) and pHPZC describe how surface charge responds to changes in solution pH, the EPZC provides insight into how the surface charge of an electrode responds to an applied electric potential [10]. It also reflects how the surface potential varies with changes in both the electrode’s surface chemistry [[11], [12], [13], [14]] and the pH of the electrolyte [12,[15], [16], [17], [18]]. AC serves as an exemplary benchmark for the investigation of pHPZC, pH(I), and EPZC because of its exceptional structural versatility and surface chemistry tunability. Unlike mono-structured carbon nanomaterials, AC simultaneously encompasses micropores, mesopores, and macropores, and its surface functional groups can be systematically introduced or altered via oxidation or heat treatments [19,20]. These characteristics make it an excellent reference system for exploring the interrelationship between pHPZC, pH(I), and EPZC values because they encompass the key physicochemical phenomena (surface charge development, functional group introduction, and electrochemical double-layer formation) that are common to other carbon-based materials such as carbon blacks, graphene derivatives, and carbon nanotubes [21,22]. While these materials differ in morphology and conductivity, the fundamental principles governing surface charge and electrochemical behavior remain analogous [23]. Consequently, data derived from AC serve as a robust foundation for extrapolating to other carbonaceous systems, particularly in the context of adsorption performance and electrochemical applications. Published in final edited form as: ACS ES T Eng. 2023 Mar 20;3(7):989–1000. doi: 10.1021/acsestengg.3c00012 Abstract Millions of households still rely on drinking water from private wells or municipal systems with arsenic levels approaching or exceeding regulatory limits. Arsenic is a potent carcinogen, and there is no safe level of it in drinking water. Point-of-use (POU) treatment systems are a promising option to mitigate arsenic exposure. However, the most commonly used POU technology, an activated carbon block filter, is ineffective at removing arsenic. Our study aimed to explore the potential of impregnating carbon blocks with amorphous titanium (hydr)oxide (THO) to improve arsenic removal without introducing titanium (Ti) into the treated water. Four synthesis methods achieved 8–16 wt.% Ti loading within the carbon block with 58–97% amorphous THO content. The THO-modified carbon block could adsorb both oxidation states of arsenic (arsenate and arsenite) in batch or column tests. Modified carbon block with higher Ti and amorphous content always led to better arsenate removal, achieving arsenic loadings up to 31 mg As/mg Ti after 70,000 bed volumes in continuous flow tests. Impregnating carbon block with amorphous THO consistently outperformed impregnation using crystalline TiO2. The best-performing system (TTIP-EtOH carbon block) was an amorphous THO derived using titanium isopropoxide, ethanol, and acetic acid via sol-gel technique, aged at 80° for 18 hours and dried overnight at 60°. Comparable pore size distribution and surface area of the impregnated carbon blocks suggested that chemical properties play a more crucial role than physical and textural properties in removing arsenate via amorphous Ti-impregnated carbon block. Freundlich isotherms indicated energetically favorable adsorption for amorphous chemically synthesized adsorbents. The mass transport coefficients for the amorphous TTIP-EtOH carbon block were fitted using a pore surface diffusion model, resulting in Dsurface = 3.1×10−12 cm2/s and Dpore = 3.2×10−6 cm2/s. Impregnating the carbon block with THO enabled effective arsenic removal from water without adversely affecting the pressure drop across the unit or the carbon block’s ability to remove polar organic chemical pollutants efficiently. Introduction Arsenic occurs in many groundwater and surface water sources across the globe 1, and it is among the top 10 most violated water quality standards in the United States 2. Arsenic is a Class A human carcinogen, and long-term exposure to arsenic-contaminated potable water has been linked to skin, kidney, liver, and bladder cancers 3. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) and World Health Organization (WHO) have set a maximum contaminant level (MCL) of 10 μg/L for arsenic in drinking water 4. As a carcinogen with a high MCL relative to cancer risk (i.e., 1 in 10,000 health risk instead of 1 in 1,000,000) there is no safe level for arsenic. Arsenic arguably poses among the highest cancer risks in drinking water 2. While drinking water systems comply with the 10 μg/L for arsenic, the regulation can be based on a very limited number of samples (e.g., less than one sample per year for small utilities), and many communities have arsenic levels near the MCL. Over 40 million people in the USA rely upon private wells that are rarely measured and not regulated for arsenic, but drinking water arsenic exposures are known to occur 5,6. Globally, arsenic concentrations exceeding the WHO regulations in drinking water may impact more than 200 million people 7. Thus, reducing arsenic exposure levels in tap water remains an important societal need. Arsenic occurs in the two inorganic oxidation states of arsenate (As(V)) and arsenite (As(III)). Because of their pKa values, arsenate occurs as a deprotonated oxo-anion at normal drinking water pH levels whereas arsenite is non-ionic and more challenging to remove without an oxidation step. Many iron, aluminum, titanium, cerium, zirconium, or other metal (hydr)oxides based adsorbents are effective in adsorbing arsenate 8,9. The adsorbent type and pore structure significantly influence arsenate removal capability 10,11. In the USA, the commercial materials most used by municipalities are iron (hydr)oxide or crystalline titanium dioxide (TiO2)-based sorbents 12–14. Titanium (hydr)oxides (THO) are stable under environmentally-relevant pH conditions 15 and can form inner-sphere complexation with arsenate through oxygen bridges 16,17. In-situ THO synthesis through hydrolysis/precipitation 18 or sol-gel methods allow flexibility to use different procedures and titanium precursors 19 that lead to formation of THO with different physico-chemical characteristics and tunable degrees of crystallinity 8. Consequently, there is a gap in studying the mechanisms of arsenate immobilization by different amorphous grades of THO. Furthermore, using high surface area (nano) powders of amorphous THO is not practical for water treatment applications of its poor hydraulic stability or need for post-filtration to remove particulates 21. Therefore, THO immobilization into a porous support is a prerequisite. Integration of nano-structured THO into pores of macro-scale adsorbents that have good hydraulic performance is an appropriate alternative22. fetched_contents.text: Equilibrium, kinetics and thermodynamic studies for adsorption of As(III) on activated alumina Introduction Arsenic is an ubiquitous element in the earth’s crust and ranks 20th among most abundant element [1]. Arsenic occurs in both organic and inorganic forms in natural waters but organic arsenic is of little importance as it goes through bio transformation and detoxifies through methylation. Inorganic arsenic occurs in −3, 0, +3, and +5 oxidation states in aquatic systems. The elemental state −3 and 0 are extremely rare whereas +3 and +5 oxidation states are commonly found in water systems depending on the prevailing redox conditions. Under reducing environment As(III) is found primarily as H3AsO3, H2AsO3−, HAsO32−, and AsO33− whereas different hydrolysis species of As(V) such as H3AsO4, H2AsO4−, HAsO42−, and AsO43− can be present in water with dissolved oxygen/oxidizing environment [2]. Although environmental restrictions and regulations have limited the production and uses of arsenic and its compounds, they are still extensively used in metallurgy, agriculture, forestry, electronics, pharmaceuticals, glass, and ceramic industry. It is introduced into the environment through weathering of rocks, mine tailings, industrial wastes discharge, fertilizers, agricultural employments of pesticides, smelting of metals, and burnings of fossil fuels [3], [4]. Inorganic species of arsenic [As(III) and As(V)] represent a potential threat to the environment, human health, and animal health due to their carcinogenic and other effects. Arsenic has been classified as a carcinogen by the USEPA. Several diseases have been linked to the consumption of arsenic containing groundwater in Bangladesh, Taiwan, Argentina, Mexico, Chile, China, Hungary, Thailand, USA, New Zealand, South Africa, and in India [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Presence of arsenic in drinking water increases the risk of skin, lung, kidney, and bladder cancer. Considering its health and toxicological effects, many regulatory agencies have revised the maximum contaminant level (MCL) for arsenic in drinking water from 0.05 to 0.01 mg l−1. Present drinking water standard for arsenic in many developing countries is 0.05 mg l−1 whereas in developed countries like Germany and USA it is 0.01 mg l−1 [10]. This permissible limit differs from country to country depending upon the facility to speculate low quantities of arsenic. Various technologies such as adsorption, ion exchange, precipitation, coagulation and filtration, reverse osmosis, and electro-dialysis have been developed for the removal of arsenic from water [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16] and reported that As(V) can be more easily removed from water than As(III) due to its divalent species but As(III) is more toxic and mobile. Thus, there is an urgent need to develop techniques which are effective for As(III) removal. Adsorption of As(III) on coconut husk carbon, carbon from fly ash, iron oxide coated polymeric material, and hybrid polymeric sorbent were investigated [17], [18], [19], [20], [21]. Attempts have been made by using iron and iron coated sand, iron coated activated carbon [8], [22], and granular ferric hydroxides [23], however, due to high operation cost, sludge, and technical difficulties in preparation of materials, their use is limited. Use of naturally occurring ores and minerals, namely, kaolinite [24] and hematite and feldspar [25] has also been examined for adsorption of arsenic though not as extensively as other materials. Activated alumina is another such adsorbent which has a great affinity for various organic and inorganic pollutants and can be easily regenerated and reused. It has been reported that activated alumina has been effective for As(V) removal [6], [26]. The aim of this work is to evaluate the effectiveness of activated alumina for the removal of As(III) from water and to investigate the parameters affecting As(III) removal. fetched_contents.text: In situ arsenic speciation at the soil/water interface of saline-alkaline lakes of the Pantanal, Brazil: A DGT-based approach Highlights * • DGT was applied in field to monitor arsenic speciation at the soil/water interface. * • High total dissolved As concentrations (mg L−1) were found in aqueous samples, whereas low concentrations were found in soils. * • As(V) was the main species in shallow water table samples collected manually. * • As(III) was the main species when sampling was carried out by DGT. * • The dynamic of arsenic at the soil/water interface is controlled by the evapoconcentration process ongoing in Pantanal. Abstract Arsenic (As) is a naturally occurring element in the Earth's crust, exhibiting toxicity towards a wide range of living organisms. Its properties and environmental dynamics are strongly regulated by its speciation, and the species As(III) and As(V) are the most commonly found in environmental systems. Recently, high concentrations of As were found in saline-alkaline lakes of the Pantanal (Brazil), which is the largest wetland area in the world. Therefore, we evaluated As contamination and its redox speciation (As(III) and As(V)) at the soil/water interface of biogeochemically distinct saline-alkaline lakes of Pantanal wetlands (Brazil). Both conventional sampling and in situ diffusive gradients in thin films (DGT) technique were employed. Zirconium oxide and 3-mercaptopropyl were used as ligand phases in DGT to selectively bind As species. High concentrations of total dissolved As in a shallow water table were found (<2337.5 μg L−1), whereas levels in soils were up to 2.4 μg g−1. Distinct scenarios were observed when comparing speciation analysis through spot sampling and DGT. Considering spot sampling, As(V) was the main species detected, whereas As(III) was only detected in only a few samples (<4.2 μg L−1). Conversely, results obtained by DGT showed that labile As(III) dominated arsenic speciation at the soil/water interface with levels up to 203.0 μg L−1. Coupling DGT data and DGT induced fluxes in sediments and soils model allowed obtaining kinetic data, showing that the soil barely participated in the arsenic dynamics on the shore of the lakes, and that this participation depends on the evapoconcentration process occurring in the region. Therefore, soil acts like a nonreactive matrix depending on the natural concentration process. In addition, our results reinforced the different geochemical characteristics of the studied saline-alkaline lakes and highlights the importance of robust passive sampling techniques in the context of metal/metalloid speciation in environmental analysis. Introduction Arsenic is a ubiquitous metalloid in the Earth's crust, being present in many minerals and distributed in environmental compartments such as water, soil, sediments, and biota. It is toxic, and carcinogenic, mainly in its inorganic forms and is considered a global health concern. It is estimated that about 94 to 220 million people around the world are potentially exposed to levels higher than the World Health Organization (World Health Organization, 2017) threshold concentration (10 μg L−1) in groundwater for their domestic water supply (Podgorski and Berg, 2020). Arsenic occurs in four oxidation states, namely +V (arsenate), +III (arsenite), 0 (arsenic), and −III (arsine) (Sharma and Sohn, 2009). Its toxicity, fate, and bioavailability are intrinsically related to its chemical species. The species As(III), As(V), monomethylarsonic and dimethylarsinic acids are the most likely to occur in natural water, and the two inorganic arsenic oxyanions, i.e. arsenite and arsenate, are the major arsenic species found in most waters, soils, and sediments (Liu and Cai, 2007). Arsenic speciation in environmental matrices highly depends on pH, electrical conductivity, and organic matter content (Sharma and Sohn, 2009). Moreover, various inorganic and organic arsenic compounds may be further combined with inorganic (e.g., Fe and Mn oxides) or organic ligands (e.g., thiol group and humic substances) to produce coordination complexes with different degrees of thermodynamic stability and lability (Liu and Cai, 2007). The availability and mobility of different arsenic species is an important factor to consider when analyzing the impact of this metalloid in a given environmental system. In this sense, passive sampling can be considered a suitable alternative to spot sampling (e.g. using containers for water sampling) since the analytes are sampled in situ, minimizing perturbations in the system (Viana et al., 2021). The diffusive gradients in thin films (DGT) technique (Davison and Zhang, 1994) is one of the most widespread passive sampling strategies due to characteristics such as (a) simplicity of deployment; (b) ease of data processing; (c) applicability to different matrixes (soil, water, and sediment); (d) sampling of a wide range of analytes; (e) assessment of some elements' speciation (Zhang and Davison, 2015). The key concept of DGT in soils and sediments is that this device acts by inducing a local and controlled perturbation into the matrix and therefore inducing an ion flux from the solid phase to the DGT resin. The resultant measurements, in terms of concentration, can then be treated to represent the soil/sediment response to the perturbation (Harper et al., 1998). DGT induced fluxes in sediments model (DIFS) allowed quantitative interpretation of DGT measurements in terms of fundamental kinetic and equilibrium resupply parameters (Harper et al., 2000). How surface charge affects arsenic adsorption efficiency?

Surface charge affects arsenic adsorption efficiency by controlling whether electrostatic attraction or repulsion dominates the interaction between the adsorbent and the adsorbate. The evidence indicates that electrostatic effects are important because the surface charge of activated carbon changes with pH, and this directly influences the adsorption behavior [N1-F1][N4-R4]. In particular, when the solution pH differs from the pHzpc, electrostatic interactions become significant, which can either enhance or hinder adsorption depending on the relative charges of the surface and the arsenic species [N6-R4]. This means that a positive surface charge may attract negatively charged arsenic species, while a negative surface charge may repel them or reduce adsorption capacity.

pH-dependent surface charge changes both adsorption capacity and selectivity. Experimental studies show that pH strongly affects arsenic removal; for example, one study reports that arsenic removal by Fe-modified activated carbon was most effective for arsenate in the pH range 2.0–12.0, suggesting that the optimal adsorption window depends on the surface charge state [N3-R3]. Another study found that As(III) and As(V) adsorption were both minimal at pH 12 and increased again at higher pH values, indicating that charge effects can shift adsorption efficiency in a nonlinear way [N3-R4]. The evidence also shows that adsorption capacity can vary with pH: activated alumina achieved maximum As(III) adsorption in the pH range 6.0–8.0, while low adsorption was observed at higher pH values [N3-F3]. This supports the conclusion that pH-dependent surface charge is a major determinant of adsorption capacity and selectivity [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R3].

Surface charge can also influence accessibility of active sites or diffusion. The review states that surface charge behavior controls adsorption behavior by affecting electrostatic interactions, and that surface chemistry critically impacts pH(I), pHPZC, and EPZC values [N1-F1]. This implies that charge changes can alter the local environment around active sites, potentially affecting diffusion and the rate at which arsenic reaches them. The evidence also emphasizes that adsorbent properties such as surface chemistry and structure are important for adsorption performance [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that a more favorable charge state may expose more active sites or improve the accessibility of sites that are otherwise blocked by electrostatic repulsion [N1-F1][N6-R4].

Modified activated carbon differs in charge behavior and adsorption because surface functional groups can be altered, which changes the acidic/basic character of the surface. The evidence notes that activated carbon can be systematically introduced or altered via oxidation or heat treatments, and that functional groups determine the surface’s electrostatic properties [N1-F1][N4-R4]. A study on P-doped activated carbon shows that modification can generate new functional groups such as C-O-P, C-P-O, and C3-P-O, which likely shift the surface charge state [N4-R1]. Another study explicitly connects oxygen-containing surface functional groups to adsorption behavior, showing that such groups can promote adsorption by enhancing neighboring carbon atom activity rather than simply through electrostatic attraction [N4-R5]. This means that modified activated carbon can exhibit different charge states and thus different adsorption efficiencies depending on the type and density of functional groups [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R5].

Overall, surface charge determines arsenic adsorption efficiency by controlling whether electrostatic attraction or repulsion dominates, by shifting adsorption capacity and selectivity with pH, by influencing site accessibility and diffusion, and by altering adsorption behavior through functional group modification [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R3][N6-R4][N4-R4][N4-R5].

How arsenic speciation and solution chemistry jointly determine adsorption performance?

Arsenic speciation shifts with pH and strongly affects adsorbability. The evidence shows that As(III) and As(V) have different speciation behavior: As(V) tends to occur as a deprotonated oxo-anion at normal drinking water pH, while As(III) is non-ionic and more challenging to remove without an oxidation step [N3-F3]. Another source states that pH determines the concentration distribution of ionic forms of arsenic species, and that speciation is strongly regulated by pH, electrical conductivity, and organic matter content [N5-F4]. The in situ speciation study in saline-alkaline lakes further reports that As(V) is the main species in shallow water table samples, whereas As(III) dominates when sampling is carried out by DGT [N5-F4]. This indicates that pH can shift arsenic between species that are more or less available for adsorption, with important implications for adsorbability [N3-F3][N5-F4].

Surface charge interacts with different arsenic species through electrostatic effects. The literature explicitly links surface charge to adsorption by stating that when the solution pH differs from the pHzpc, electrostatic interactions become significant [N6-R4]. For arsenic, this means that a positively charged surface may attract negatively charged arsenate species, while a negatively charged surface may repel them or reduce adsorption capacity [N1-F1]. The mechanistic study of arsenate adsorption on amorphous titanium (hydr)oxides reports inner-sphere complexation through oxygen bridging, which suggests that surface oxygen groups can bind arsenate directly rather than only through electrostatic attraction [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that arsenic speciation and surface charge jointly determine adsorption: speciation defines the adsorbate’s chemical form, while surface charge defines the electrostatic environment that favors or disfavors binding [N2-F2][N6-R4].

pH-dependent competition with other ions or background electrolytes matters because solution chemistry can alter the adsorption environment. The evidence shows that arsenic adsorption is affected by pH, adsorbent dose, and contact time, and that the adsorption mechanism can involve both electrostatic attraction and inner-sphere complexation [N3-F3][N2-R5]. A separate study on arsenic speciation emphasizes that solution chemistry is strongly regulated by pH, electrical conductivity, and organic matter content, implying that background electrolytes and other ions can compete for adsorption sites or modify the effective charge environment [N5-F4]. The activated alumina study also shows that adsorption strongly depends on pH, which indirectly implies that other ions and electrolytes can influence the observed adsorption capacity [N3-F3]. Therefore, solution chemistry is not a passive backdrop; it actively mediates the adsorption process by changing the relative availability of adsorbate species and the competition for surface sites [N5-F4][N3-F3].

Oxidation/reduction and speciation changes also affect adsorption behavior. The evidence indicates that As(III) can be oxidized to As(V) under certain conditions, and that oxidation can occur at or above pH 9.2 above the first pKa of H3AsO3 [N5-R5]. This is important because As(V) is generally easier to remove than As(III) due to its divalent species, but As(III) is more toxic and mobile [N3-F3]. The speciation study also notes that uncharged H3AsO3 species occur under reducing conditions, while AsO4^3− and H3AsO4 are present in strong alkaline and acidic solutions, respectively [N5-R2]. This means that oxidation/reduction conditions can shift arsenic between species that are more or less favorable for adsorption, and that speciation changes can therefore alter adsorption behavior significantly [N5-R2][N5-R5][N3-F3].

In summary, arsenic speciation and solution chemistry jointly determine adsorption performance by shifting the dominant arsenic species with pH, by enabling electrostatic interactions or inner-sphere complexation depending on surface charge, by introducing competition from other ions or electrolytes, and by allowing oxidation/reduction changes that alter adsorbability [N3-F3][N5-F4][N2-F2][N6-R4][N5-R2][N5-R5].

What determines the surface charge of activated carbon at different pHs?

Activated carbon surface charge is determined by its surface chemistry, particularly the presence of functional groups, oxygen-containing groups, and the balance between acidic and basic surface sites. Boehm titration is a central method for defining surface charge because it measures the amounts of acidic and basic oxygen functionalities on the surface [N1-R5]. The point of zero charge (pHzpc) is another key metric, representing the pH at which the net surface charge is zero and thus the threshold where surface protonation/deprotonation changes sign [N1-F1]. In activated carbon, this means that surface charge depends directly on solution pH: below pHzpc, the surface becomes positively charged; above pHzpc, it becomes negatively charged [N1-F1].

Zeta potential is closely related to colloidal stability and surface ionization. The literature explicitly states that the isoelectric point (pH(I)) is the pH at which zeta potential is zero, and that pH(I) provides complementary insight into surface charge compared to pHzpc [N1-F1]. For porous solids like activated carbon, pH(I) is usually lower than pHzpc, which reflects the interplay between surface charge and the porous structure [N1-F1]. Zeta potential therefore captures the effective electrostatic charge of the surface in aqueous solution, including the effects of ionization and the surrounding electrolyte [N1-F1].

Functional groups and oxygen-containing groups are the main contributors to surface charge. Boehm titration and surface chemistry characterization show that activated carbon contains acidic and basic oxygen functionalities, and that these groups define the surface’s electrostatic behavior [N1-R5][N1-R4]. More broadly, oxygen-containing functional groups are described as the chemical moieties that dictate adsorbate affinity, and their presence can change the surface’s ability to interact with ions and molecules [N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that modification of activated carbon can introduce new functional groups, such as C-O-P, C-P-O, and C3-P-O, which further alter surface chemistry and charge state [N4-R1]. In other words, activated carbon’s surface charge is not static; it is shaped by oxygenated groups, hydroxyls, and other functional groups that can protonate or deprotonate depending on pH [N4-R4][N4-R5].

pH-dependent protonation/deprotonation changes the surface charge state in a systematic way. At lower pH, acidic oxygen groups can be protonated, increasing positive surface charge; at higher pH, deprotonation occurs, leading to negative surface charge [N1-F1]. The review explicitly says that the magnitude of surface charge depends on pH, and that the pH at which the net surface charge is zero is the pHzpc [N1-F1]. This means that the surface charge state is a dynamic function of pH, with strong implications for adsorption and electrostatic interactions [N1-F1].

Overall, activated carbon surface charge is best understood through Boehm titration and pHzpc measurements as defining the surface’s acidic/basic character, zeta potential as reflecting colloidal stability and ionization, and functional groups as the chemical basis for charge generation. pH controls the protonation/deprotonation of those groups, so the surface charge state changes continuously with pH [N1-F1][N1-R5][N4-R4].

Evidence for a specific pH optimum and how it is explained by charge and speciation

The available evidence suggests that arsenic adsorption on activated carbon often shows a pH optimum, and that this optimum is best explained by the combined effects of surface charge and arsenic speciation rather than by a single factor alone. The experimental studies consistently show that adsorption efficiency varies strongly with pH. For example, one study reports that arsenic removal by Fe-modified activated carbon was most effective for arsenate in the pH range 2.0–12.0 [N3-R3], while another reports that As(III) and As(V) adsorption were both minimal at pH 12 and increased again at higher pH values [N3-R4]. Activated alumina also achieved maximum As(III) adsorption in the pH range 6.0–8.0, with lower adsorption observed at higher pH values [N3-F3]. These results indicate that adsorption efficiency does not simply rise or fall monotonically with pH; instead, there are specific regions where the adsorbent and adsorbate interact most favorably.

The optimum differs between As(III) and As(V) because their speciation and charge behavior are different. ## Integrated explanation of how pH affects activated carbon surface charge and arsenic adsorption efficiency

### 1. How pH determines activated carbon surface charge

The surface charge of activated carbon is fundamentally determined by its surface chemistry and pH-dependent protonation/deprotonation behavior. Boehm titration is a central method for defining surface charge because it measures the amounts of acidic and basic oxygen functionalities present on the surface [N1-R5]. The point of zero charge (pHzpc) is also central: it represents the pH at which the net surface charge is zero, and thus it marks the threshold where surface protonation/deprotonation changes sign [N1-F1]. At lower pH, acidic oxygen groups can be protonated, increasing positive surface charge; at higher pH, deprotonation occurs, leading to negative surface charge [N1-F1].

Zeta potential is closely related to colloidal stability and surface ionization. The isoelectric point (pH(I)) is the pH at which zeta potential is zero, and it provides complementary insight into surface charge compared to pHzpc [N1-F1]. For porous solids like activated carbon, pH(I) is usually lower than pHzpc, reflecting the interplay between surface charge and the porous structure [N1-F1]. Zeta potential therefore captures the effective electrostatic charge of the surface in aqueous solution, including the effects of ionization and the surrounding electrolyte [N1-F1].

Functional groups and oxygen-containing groups are the main contributors to surface charge. Boehm titration and surface chemistry characterization show that activated carbon contains acidic and basic oxygen functionalities, and that these groups define the surface’s electrostatic behavior [N1-R5][N1-R4]. More broadly, oxygen-containing functional groups are described as the chemical moieties that dictate adsorbate affinity, and their presence can change the surface’s ability to interact with ions and molecules [N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that modification of activated carbon can introduce new functional groups, such as C-O-P, C-P-O, and C3-P-O, which further alter surface chemistry and charge state [N4-R1]. In other words, activated carbon’s surface charge is not static; it is shaped by oxygenated groups, hydroxyls, and other functional groups that can protonate or deprotonate depending on pH [N4-R4][N4-R5].

### 2. How surface charge affects arsenic adsorption efficiency

Surface charge affects arsenic adsorption efficiency by controlling whether electrostatic attraction or repulsion dominates the interaction between the adsorbent and the adsorbate. The evidence indicates that electrostatic effects are important because the surface charge of activated carbon changes with pH, and this directly influences the adsorption behavior [N1-F1][N4-R4]. In particular, when the solution pH differs from the pHzpc, electrostatic interactions become significant, which can either enhance or hinder adsorption depending on the relative charges of the surface and the arsenic species [N6-R4]. This means that a positive surface charge may attract negatively charged arsenic species, while a negative surface charge may repel them or reduce adsorption capacity.

pH-dependent surface charge changes both adsorption capacity and selectivity. Experimental studies show that pH strongly affects arsenic removal; for example, one study reports that arsenic removal by Fe-modified activated carbon was most effective for arsenate in the pH range 2.0–12.0 [N3-R3]. Another study found that As(III) and As(V) adsorption were both minimal at pH 12 and increased again at higher pH values, indicating that charge effects can shift adsorption efficiency in a nonlinear way [N3-R4]. The evidence also shows that adsorption capacity can vary with pH: activated alumina achieved maximum As(III) adsorption in the pH range 6.0–8.0, while low adsorption was observed at higher pH values [N3-F3]. This supports the conclusion that pH-dependent surface charge is a major determinant of adsorption capacity and selectivity [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R3].

Surface charge can also influence accessibility of active sites or diffusion. The review states that surface charge behavior controls adsorption behavior by affecting electrostatic interactions, and that surface chemistry critically impacts pH(I), pHPZC, and EPZC values [N1-F1]. This implies that charge changes can alter the local environment around active sites, potentially affecting diffusion and the rate at which arsenic reaches them. The evidence also emphasizes that adsorbent properties such as surface chemistry and structure are important for adsorption performance [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that a more favorable charge state may expose more active sites or improve the accessibility of sites that are otherwise blocked by electrostatic repulsion [N1-F1][N6-R4].

Modified activated carbon differs in charge behavior and adsorption because surface functional groups can be altered, which changes the acidic/basic character of the surface. The evidence notes that activated carbon can be systematically introduced or altered via oxidation or heat treatments, and that functional groups determine the surface’s electrostatic properties [N1-F1][N4-R4]. A study on P-doped activated carbon shows that modification can generate new functional groups such as C-O-P, C-P-O, and C3-P-O, which likely shift the surface charge state [N4-R1]. Another study explicitly connects oxygen-containing surface functional groups to adsorption behavior, showing that such groups can promote adsorption by enhancing neighboring carbon atom activity rather than simply through electrostatic attraction [N4-R5]. This means that modified activated carbon can exhibit different charge states and thus different adsorption efficiencies depending on the type and density of functional groups [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R5].

### 3. How arsenic speciation and solution chemistry jointly determine adsorption performance

Arsenic speciation shifts with pH and strongly affects adsorbability. The evidence shows that As(III) and As(V) have different speciation behavior: As(V) tends to occur as a deprotonated oxo-anion at normal drinking water pH, while As(III) is non-ionic and more challenging to remove without an oxidation step [N3-F3]. Another source states that pH determines the concentration distribution of ionic forms of arsenic species, and that speciation is strongly regulated by pH, electrical conductivity, and organic matter content [N5-F4]. The in situ speciation study in saline-alkaline lakes further reports that As(V) is the main species in shallow water table samples, whereas As(III) dominates when sampling is carried out by DGT [N5-F4]. This indicates that pH can shift arsenic between species that are more or less available for adsorption, with important implications for adsorbability [N3-F3][N5-F4].

Surface charge interacts with different arsenic species through electrostatic effects. The literature explicitly links surface charge to adsorption by stating that when the solution pH differs from the pHzpc, electrostatic interactions become significant [N6-R4]. For arsenic, this means that a positively charged surface may attract negatively charged arsenate species, while a negatively charged surface may repel them or reduce adsorption capacity [N1-F1]. The mechanistic study of arsenate adsorption on amorphous titanium (hydr)oxides reports inner-sphere complexation through oxygen bridging, which suggests that surface oxygen groups can bind arsenate directly rather than only through electrostatic attraction [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that arsenic speciation and surface charge jointly determine adsorption: speciation defines the adsorbate’s chemical form, while surface charge defines the electrostatic environment that favors or disfavors binding [N2-F2][N6-R4].

pH-dependent competition with other ions or background electrolytes matters because solution chemistry can alter the adsorption environment. The evidence shows that arsenic adsorption is affected by pH, adsorbent dose, and contact time, and that the adsorption mechanism can involve both electrostatic attraction and inner-sphere complexation [N3-F3][N2-R5]. A separate study on arsenic speciation emphasizes that solution chemistry is strongly regulated by pH, electrical conductivity, and organic matter content, implying that background electrolytes and other ions can compete for adsorption sites or modify the effective charge environment [N5-F4]. The activated alumina study also shows that adsorption strongly depends on pH, which indirectly implies that other ions and electrolytes can influence the observed adsorption capacity [N3-F3]. Therefore, solution chemistry is not a passive backdrop; it actively mediates the adsorption process by changing the relative availability of adsorbate species and the competition for surface sites [N5-F4][N3-F3].

Oxidation/reduction and speciation changes also affect adsorption behavior. The evidence indicates that As(III) can be oxidized to As(V) under certain conditions, and that oxidation can occur at or above pH 9.2 above the first pKa of H3AsO3 [N5-R5]. This is important because As(V) is generally easier to remove than As(III) due to its divalent species, but As(III) is more toxic and mobile [N3-F3]. The speciation study also notes that uncharged H3AsO3 species occur under reducing conditions, while AsO4^3− and H3AsO4 are present in strong alkaline and acidic solutions, respectively [N5-R2]. This means that oxidation/reduction conditions can shift arsenic between species that are more or less favorable for adsorption, and that speciation changes can therefore alter adsorption behavior significantly [N5-R2][N5-R5][N3-F3].

### 4. Evidence for a specific pH optimum and why it exists

The available evidence suggests that arsenic adsorption on activated carbon often shows a pH optimum, and that this optimum is best explained by the combined effects of surface charge and arsenic speciation rather than by a single factor alone. The experimental studies consistently show that adsorption efficiency varies strongly with pH. For example, one study reports that arsenic removal by Fe-modified activated carbon was most effective for arsenate in the pH range 2.0–12.0 [N3-R3], while another reports that As(III) and As(V) adsorption were both minimal at pH 12 and increased again at higher pH values [N3-R4]. Activated alumina also achieved maximum As(III) adsorption in the pH range 6.0–8.0, with lower adsorption observed at higher pH values [N3-F3]. These results indicate that adsorption efficiency does not simply rise or fall monotonically with pH; instead, there are specific regions where the adsorbent and adsorbate interact most favorably.

The optimum differs between As(III) and As(V) because their speciation and charge behavior are different. As(V) is reported to occur as a deprotonated oxo-anion at normal drinking water pH, while As(III) is non-ionic and more difficult to remove without an oxidation step [N3-F3]. Another source notes that uncharged H3AsO3 species occur under reducing conditions, while AsO4^3− and H3AsO4 are present in strong alkaline and acidic solutions, respectively [N5-R2]. This means that As(V) tends to exist in a more charge-sensitive form across the pH range, whereas As(III) may be more mobile and less readily bound under certain conditions [N3-F3][N5-R2]. The evidence also shows that oxidation of As(III) to As(V) can occur at or above pH 9.2 above the first pKa of H3AsO3 [N5-R5], which further explains why As(V) is generally easier to remove than As(III) [N3-F3]. Together, these findings support the idea that the pH optimum for As(V) is often different from that for As(III), because each species responds differently to solution chemistry and surface charge [N3-F3][N5-R2][N5-R5].

Experimental data support the idea that a simple charge-speciation model is incomplete. The evidence shows that arsenic adsorption involves more than just electrostatic attraction: it also involves inner-sphere complexation through oxygen bridging, as observed in mechanistic studies of arsenate adsorption on amorphous titanium (hydr)oxides [N2-F2]. Another study indicates that the removal mechanism involves a combination of electrostatic attraction and inner-sphere complexation [N2-R5]. This means that adsorption is jointly governed by surface charge, speciation, and the nature of the interaction between the adsorbate and the adsorbent surface. The available evidence does not contradict a charge-speciation model; instead, it suggests that such a model must include electrostatic effects, inner-sphere/outer-sphere interactions, and speciation shifts with pH [N2-F2][N2-R5][N5-R2][N5-R5].

### 5. How electrostatics, inner-sphere/outer-sphere mechanisms, and speciation work together

Electrostatics, inner-sphere/outer-sphere mechanisms, and speciation all play together to determine adsorption behavior. Surface charge is central because it controls whether electrostatic attraction or repulsion dominates [N1-F1][N6-R4]. The literature explicitly links surface charge to adsorption by stating that when the solution pH differs from the pHzpc, electrostatic interactions become significant [N6-R4]. At the same time, inner-sphere complexation provides a direct chemical binding pathway, especially for arsenate, where surface oxygen groups can form oxygen-bridged complexes [N2-F2]. Speciation matters because pH determines the dominant arsenic species, and different species interact differently with the surface [N3-F3][N5-F4]. The evidence also shows that oxidation/reduction changes can shift arsenic between As(III) and As(V), further altering adsorbability [N5-R5]. Thus, the overall adsorption optimum arises from the interplay of these factors: a favorable surface charge state, a species form that can bind effectively, and a mechanism that combines electrostatic attraction with inner-sphere complexation [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-R2][N5-R5].

### 6. Bottom line

In summary, pH affects activated carbon surface charge by changing the protonation/deprotonation state of functional groups and oxygen-containing groups, with Boehm titration and pHzpc measurements providing the key experimental framework [N1-R5][N1-F1]. Surface charge then influences arsenic adsorption efficiency by controlling electrostatic attraction or repulsion, changing adsorption capacity and selectivity, and affecting the accessibility of active sites [N1-F1][N4-R4][N6-R4]. At the same time, arsenic speciation and solution chemistry are critical because they determine which arsenic species are present, how they interact with the surface, and whether oxidation/reduction changes alter adsorbability [N3-F3][N5-F4][N5-R2][N5-R5]. The evidence supports a specific pH optimum for adsorption, but this optimum emerges from the combined effects of surface charge, speciation, and adsorption mechanisms such as electrostatic attraction and inner-sphere complexation [N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-F3][N2-F2][N2-R5][N5-R2][N5-R5].
